title: Co-creation and Facilitation
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Co-creation and Facilitation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Co-creation brings people with different forms of expertise into the design process: customers, frontline staff, operations, subject experts, engineers, and leaders. Facilitation creates the conditions for them to contribute, disagree productively, and make evidence visible.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose participants deliberately, provide accessible materials, state the purpose and decision boundary, and distinguish brainstorming from commitment. Inclusion is not inviting everyone into a room; it is ensuring relevant perspectives can shape the work.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design participation as carefully as the workshop
turns.text: What changes when we look at design participation as carefully as the workshop?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The session separates four modes. First, participants inspect shared evidence and correct the current-state model. Second, individuals map failures privately so hierarchy cannot set the opening frame. Third, mixed groups generate and rehearse alternatives.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Fourth, options are assessed against visible criteria: patient progress, safety, equity, capacity, feasibility, privacy, and recoverability. Voting can surface preference, but it does not settle a trade-off whose consequences fall unevenly.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: redesigning school enrolment?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Parents, administrators, teachers, accessibility specialists, and policy staff each hold a different part of enrolment. A productive workshop lets families expose evidence and timing burdens, staff explain exception work, and policy owners distinguish fixed rules from inherited habit.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It does not ask parents to design a form or pretend a majority vote can override safeguarding duties.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design the participation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: State the decision participants can influence, the evidence they bring, and what remains outside the session. Invite people across customer, frontline, operational, policy, technical, and partner perspectives without pretending unequal power disappears in a workshop. Make participation accessible and compensate lived expertise where appropriate.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use individual reflection, structured sharing, mapping, scenario critique, and prioritisation tied to criteria. Prevent dominant voices from setting the frame; separate idea generation from evaluation. Surface disagreements and assumptions rather than forcing cheerful consensus.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Close with decisions, open questions, owners, and how outputs will be used. Return outcomes to participants. Facilitation is ethical when people understand why they are involved and can see their contribution influence work—not when sticky notes are extracted to legitimise a predetermined plan.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Workshops can reproduce hierarchy. Use facilitation methods that make quieter, distributed, or less powerful knowledge visible rather than rewarding the loudest participant.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Co-creation is useful when no single participant holds the whole picture. Customers bring lived context; frontline staff know workarounds and failure patterns; operations understand constraints; engineers understand technical possibilities; leaders hold strategic and policy choices.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design the session around a defined question and decision boundary, then choose activities that let each form of expertise become visible without requiring people to perform design fluency.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Facilitation manages power as well as time. Provide accessible materials, clear language, pre-work where appropriate, individual reflection before group discussion, and multiple ways to contribute. Separate evidence sharing, idea generation, critique, and commitment so the loudest or most senior person does not convert a workshop into a disguised approval meeting.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Capture dissent and unresolved questions, not only consensus.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Participation theatre: affected people are invited after the important decision is fixed. Status dominance: seniority or fluency determines the output rather than relevant experience. Workshop-as-decision: brainstorming is mistaken for evidence or a committed roadmap. Inaccessible format: language, timing, materials, or tools exclude the people needed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Designers map a service without frontline staff. The map looks coherent but misses the workaround that staff use every day to protect customers from a policy gap.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Worked example In an appointment workshop, residents map constraints and recovery, staff map policy and capacity, and technologists map system limits. Each group first works separately, then compares a shared scenario. The facilitator records conflicts rather than averaging them.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Participants agree on principles and experiments, while a named service owner retains accountability for the final trade-off. The session changes the decision boundary instead of producing a wall of unactioned ideas. Blueprints reveal dependencies. Co-creation brings the knowledge needed to change them. lesson 60 tests the whole service before committing to a launch.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Notice whose perspective is absent from a product decision you know about. What risk does that absence create?
